section.title: The Second Test
section.sectionRationale: The heavenly council convenes a second time, because the first test, though devastating, did not touch Job's own flesh. Satan raises the stakes with a proverb, skin for skin, and God permits an assault on Job's body itself. The chapter ends with Job's wife's despair, Job's second refusal to sin, and the arrival of three friends whose silent sitting is the last unbroken kindness of the book before the speeches begin.
section.thesis: Even when Satan is allowed to strike Job's own body, Job still refuses to curse God, showing his integrity was never dependent on health any more than it was on wealth; his friends' seven days of silence is real comfort, soon to be squandered.
section.frameNote: Four scenes: the second council and the boil-covered test; Job's wife urging him to curse God and die; Job's reply that both good and adversity come from God's hand; and the three friends arriving to weep, tear their robes, and sit with him in silence.

units.label: The second council
units.note: you incited Me against him without cause

verses.text: On another day the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan also came with them to present himself before Him.

"Where have you come from?" said the LORD to Satan. 
"From roaming through the earth," he replied, "and walking back and forth in it."

Then the LORD said to Satan, "Have you considered My servant Job? For there is no one on earth like him, a man who is blameless and upright, who fears God and shuns evil. He still retains his {{tummah|integrity}}, even though you incited Me against him to ruin him {{chinnam|without cause}}."
"Skin for skin!" Satan replied. "A man will give up all he owns in exchange for his life.
But stretch out Your hand and strike his flesh and bones, and he will surely curse You to Your face."
"Very well," said the LORD to Satan. "He is in your hands, but you must spare his life."

units.label: Satan strikes Job's body
units.note: terrible boils from head to foot

verses.text: So Satan went out from the presence of the LORD and infected Job with terrible {{shechin|boils}} from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head.
And Job took a piece of broken pottery to scrape himself as he sat among the ashes.

units.label: Job's wife and Job's reply
units.note: should we accept only good from God

verses.text: Then Job's wife said to him, "Do you still retain your {{tummah|integrity}}? Curse God and die!"

"You speak as a {{nabal|foolish}} woman speaks," he told her. "Should we accept from God only good and not adversity?" 
In all this, Job did not sin in what he said.

units.label: The friends arrive
units.note: seven days and seven nights of silence

verses.text: Now when Job's three friends, Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite, heard about all this adversity that had come upon him, each of them came from his home, and they met together to go and sympathize with Job and comfort him.
When they lifted up their eyes from afar, they could barely recognize Job. They began to weep aloud, and each man tore his robe and threw dust in the air over his head.
Then they sat on the ground with him for seven days and seven nights, but no one spoke a word to him because they saw how intense his suffering was.

chinnam.gloss: Without cause, for nothing, gratuitously. God Himself uses this word to describe what was done to Job: real, undeserved suffering, inflicted for no fault of his own. This is one of the most theologically loaded phrases in the book, ruling out any simple explanation that Job's suffering was earned.

tummah.gloss: Integrity, blamelessness, the noun form of the same root behind tam in chapter 1. God affirms that Job still holds it after the first test; Job's wife throws the word back at him bitterly, as if integrity were now worthless.

shechin.gloss: A boil or inflamed sore, the same word used for the sixth plague on Egypt. Covering Job from head to foot, it makes him unrecognizable to his own friends and reduces him to sitting among the ashes, scraping himself with broken pottery.

nabal.gloss: A fool, not merely unintelligent but morally and spiritually senseless, one who acts as though God does not matter, as in Psalm 14:1. Job's rebuke of his wife is sharp but aimed at her counsel, not a final verdict on her character; she too has lost everything.

basic.context: The heavenly council meets again. God commends Job's continued integrity, and Satan raises the stakes with a proverb, skin for skin, arguing that Job has only been tested at a comfortable distance. God permits an attack on Job's own body, and Job is covered in boils from head to foot, sitting in ashes and scraping himself with broken pottery. His wife urges him to curse God and die; Job refuses, insisting that a life that receives good from God's hand must also be willing to receive adversity. Three friends arrive, and their first act is real kindness: they weep, they grieve visibly, and then they simply sit with him in silence for seven days.
basic.hermeneutics: God's own words are essential here: He tells Satan that Job was ruined chinnam, without cause. This closes off, before the friends ever speak, any theory that Job's suffering can be explained by some hidden sin. The chapter also shows that grief and lament are not sin; Job's silence-breaking will come next chapter, but here his restraint under unbearable pain is itself part of the book's honest witness to what faithful suffering can look like.
basic.originalLanguages: God twice affirms Job's tummah, integrity, and adds the weighty word chinnam, without cause, ruling out any notion that Job deserved this. The shechin, boils, that cover him head to foot are the same disease named among Egypt's plagues. And Job calls his wife's counsel nabal, the word for the fool who lives as if God does not exist, even while acknowledging her real suffering too.
basic.typology: The proverb 'skin for skin' anticipates a deeper truth still to come: that it will finally cost far more than skin, an entire body given over to suffering, to answer the accuser once and for all. Job's refusal to curse God even in bodily agony foreshadows a greater patience under a far worse affliction.
basic.christ: Job's body is given over to the affliction while his life is spared; Christ's body was given over to affliction and death itself, the ultimate answer to the accuser's slander that no one serves God for God's own sake. Job's silent endurance under the friends' watching eyes, before he ever speaks, faintly anticipates the silence of the suffering servant who, like a lamb before its shearers, did not open his mouth.
basic.god: God permits the escalation but still holds a boundary, Job's life must be spared. He is not indifferent to the extremity of the test, yet He also does not explain Himself to Job in this chapter or protect him from it. The tension between God's sovereignty and Job's suffering is left standing, not resolved.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 53:7 pictures the suffering servant silent before his shearers; 1 Corinthians 10:13 promises a way of escape so believers are not tested beyond what they can bear; James 5:11 points back to Job's endurance as proof that the Lord is full of compassion and mercy in the end.
basic.oneStory: The second test strips away the last possible excuse, Job's health, and still he does not curse God. His friends' seven days of silent grief are the last moment in the book where comfort is offered rightly, before human wisdom opens its mouth and starts getting it wrong.

context.literary:
Job 2 is built as a deliberate twin of Job 1. The council opens with almost the same words, Job 2:1 with Job 1:6, the same question is put to Satan and answered with the same roaming report, and the same commendation is spoken, with one addition: 'He still retains his integrity,' Job 2:3. The pattern of permission and limit repeats too, but the limit is drawn differently. In Job 1:12 the boundary was 'do not lay a hand on him'; here it is 'you must spare his life,' Job 2:6. The first round took away what Job had; the second reaches what Job is.

Within the chapter the movement is a widening circle of voices. In the heavens God and Satan speak. On the ash heap Job's wife speaks, the only time she appears in the book. Then the friends arrive, and the chapter ends not with a speech but with a silence, Job 2:13, the last quiet before the poetry begins. The narrator tells us that Job 'did not sin in what he said,' Job 2:10, and in the Hebrew the phrase 'with his lips' quietly leaves room for the question the rest of the book will ask, what Job may yet think and say.

The friends are introduced by name and by place, Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, Zophar the Naamathite, Job 2:11. That listing does two jobs. It gives the dialogue its cast, and it lets the reader watch their first gestures, the weeping, the torn robes, the dust tossed toward the sky, before their words begin. Everything they later say has to be read against the good they did here.

The chapter also tightens the book's central design. Satan's wager about motive is now fully staged, and the only way it can be answered is by Job's own mouth.
context.historical:
Job's world is the patriarchal East, a place of herds, tribes and travelling sages, with no mention of Israel's law or its sanctuary. The boils and the ash heap belong to ancient grief customs as much as to sickness. Sitting in ashes and dust was a sign of mourning across the ancient Near East and in Israel, and the friends' gestures in Job 2:12 are the same: torn robes and dust thrown up and scattered over the head. Elsewhere in Scripture the elders of Zion sit on the ground in silence with dust on their heads, Lamentations 2:10, and Ezekiel sits among the exiles for seven days, overwhelmed, Ezekiel 3:15.

Seven days was the standard span of mourning. Joseph mourned his father seven days, Genesis 50:10. The friends therefore do not simply pause out of awkwardness. They keep the full period of grief owed to someone who is, in their eyes, as good as dead. Note how much they see before they act. From afar they cannot recognise him, Job 2:12. Disease has stripped his face of everything that made him known.

The disease itself is left unnamed. The Hebrew word is shechin, the same word behind the 'festering boils' of Egypt's plague, Exodus 9:8-11, and behind the 'painful, incurable boils' from the soles of the feet to the top of the head in the covenant curses, Deuteronomy 28:35. An Israelite hearer of this story would have felt the echo. Job is in a state that Moses names as a curse, and he is not under Moses' covenant at all.

The location of the friends is a clue to their character. Teman lay in Edom, a region proverbial for wisdom, Jeremiah 49:7, so the visit is a gathering of the East's learned men at the bedside of the East's greatest man, Job 1:3.
context.canonical:
The figure of the Accuser recurs across Scripture, and Job 2 is its clearest early portrait. In Zechariah 3:1-2 Satan stands at the right hand of Joshua the high priest to accuse him, and it is the LORD who rebukes him. In Revelation 12:10 he is 'the accuser of our brothers' who accuses them 'day and night before our God,' and he is thrown down. Jesus says of Peter, 'Satan has asked to sift each of you like wheat. But I have prayed for you,' Luke 22:31-32. In each place the pattern of Job holds: the enemy needs a permission, and someone stands between him and the person he accuses.

The chapter's central question, whether a person can serve God for nothing, is answered in later Scripture by testimony rather than argument. James holds Job up as the example of perseverance and points to 'the outcome from the Lord,' James 5:11. Paul's thorn in the flesh, 'a messenger of Satan,' is given and limited by God and answered with 'My grace is sufficient for you,' 2 Corinthians 12:7-9. Both echo Job's pattern of affliction under a divine boundary with a purpose the sufferer cannot see.

Job's reply, 'Should we accept from God only good and not adversity?' Job 2:10, sits beside a line in Isaiah, 'I form the light and create the darkness; I bring prosperity and create calamity,' Isaiah 45:7, and beside the plain Hebrew idea that the one Lord stands behind both tov and ra. It also reaches forward. Every biblical lament that refuses to hand suffering to a rival god, the Psalms above all, is heir to this sentence.

Finally the chapter belongs to the book's own frame. The word for the friends' consolation in Job 2:11 returns in Job 42:11, where the family 'consoled him and comforted him.' The book begins and ends with human comfort, and the poetry between shows how badly it can go wrong.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author wanted the first hearers to learn to read suffering the way the heavenly council has already read it. The chapter hands the reader information that Job never receives: God calls the affliction 'without cause,' Job 2:3, and names the contest behind it. That advantage is deliberate. It makes every later speech of the friends a test of the reader's own theology. If we agree with their confident diagnosis we have not read Job 2.

The chapter is also meant to answer a suspicion about religion itself. Satan's charge, in Job 1:9 and again in Job 2:4-5, is that piety is a form of trade, that people worship God for what He pays. The author lets the charge be tried at its hardest point, a man's own body, and lets the answer come from Job's mouth: he receives adversity from God's hand and does not curse. Hearers in Israel who were themselves being tested were meant to take courage from this, and to see that God does not lose His servants to a wager.

Finally the author wants us to take the friends' silence seriously as a good. Before they speak they do exactly what grief asks, and the author records it without irony. What goes wrong afterwards goes wrong because they stop being present and start being wise.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records what Satan proposed, what God allowed, what Job's wife said and how Job answered. It does not tell sufferers to sit in ashes, to scrape themselves with pottery, or to expect a heavenly wager behind their own illness. The scene of the council is not offered as a template for explaining any particular pain, and Job 2 gives no licence to tell a sick person that their sickness is a test set up by Satan.

The abiding instruction is more modest. A person who belongs to God receives both good and adversity from His hand and may still hold to Him. The pattern of the friends' first week is also worth carrying forward: they come, they weep with those who weep, Romans 12:15, they sit, and they say nothing they cannot know. That is presence, not a rule about how many days to remain silent.

Two cautions belong here. The wife's counsel is recorded, not endorsed, and Job's reply is likewise reported rather than commended in every detail. And the chapter must not be turned into a formula in which every good response to suffering looks like Job's. The book as a whole allows him to lament, question and argue, and God will later say he spoke rightly of Him, Job 42:7.

debates.question: Was Job's rebuke of his wife too harsh, given that she too had lost everything?

views.label: A necessary refusal of counsel that would have led to sin
views.case: Her advice, 'Curse God and die,' Job 2:9, is exactly what Satan predicted in Job 2:5, so Job's answer is a defence of the God he serves. He also does not say she is a fool; he says she speaks 'as a foolish woman speaks,' which criticises the counsel and leaves her standing. His next sentence, 'Should we accept from God only good and not adversity?' includes her in 'we.'

views.label: A sharp word toward a woman suffering the same losses he was
views.case: She had lost the same ten children and the same fortune, and she now watches her husband rot. The text does not say she is wicked, and Job later says his breath is repulsive to his wife, Job 19:17. Calling her foolish, even if the theology is right, passes over her grief, which the story never addresses.

views.label: A woman voicing the temptation the reader is meant to feel
views.case: Some readers see her less as a character to be judged than as the last pressure in the test. Her question 'Do you still retain your integrity?' repeats God's own words about Job from Job 2:3, the verb 'retain' being the same, and turns them into mockery. The narrator gives her no other word and no later mention, which suggests her function is to sharpen the test.

debates.bearing: Whatever we decide about tone, the narrator's verdict is that Job 'did not sin in what he said.' The passage can be read for its theology without settling every question about his manner. The safest practical lesson is to refuse the counsel while staying gentle with the counsellor who is grieving beside you.

debates.question: What does 'skin for skin' mean in Satan's proverb?

views.label: A trader's principle: a man will give any skin, meaning any possession, to save his own
views.case: On this reading the proverb comes from bartering and Satan applies it to Job. Property and even children are the outer skins a man can give up; the real cost is the body. Verse 4 goes on directly, 'A man will give up all he owns in exchange for his life,' which supports it.

views.label: Like for like, a cynical saying about equivalent exchange
views.case: The Hebrew phrase is bare and can mean simply skin in exchange for skin, one loss set against another. Satan uses it to say that Job has been willing to lose others' skins and his own possessions because he was still safe himself.

views.label: A proverb about how a person shields his own skin by giving up another's
views.case: A few take it to mean that a man will let his own kin or cattle be hurt to spare his own body. The verse that follows, about giving up all he owns for his life, fits this less directly, but it explains why the second test aims at Job's own flesh and bones.

debates.bearing: The exact background of the saying is uncertain, and the chapter does not need us to fix it. On all readings the point is the same: Satan claims that self-preservation is the deepest human motive, and Job's response shows that his devotion was never bought.

study.originalLanguages:
Start with the Accuser's name. In Job 1:6 and Job 2:1 the word is ha-satan, with the definite article, so it reads 'the Accuser' or 'the Adversary,' as the BSB footnote in Job 2:1 explains. The word comes from a verb that means to oppose or to accuse. The same word without the article is used of a human enemy in some places, and in 1 Chronicles 21:1 it stands without the article as a personal name when Satan 'incited David to take a census.' In Job and in Zechariah 3:1-2 the article keeps the emphasis on the role, an adversary who works only where God allows it.

God's charge in Job 2:3 uses the verb sut, 'incited.' It is the verb of persuading or pushing someone toward an action, used of Jezebel inciting Ahab, 1 Kings 21:25. The strangeness is in God's own admission: 'you incited Me against him.' The text does not say that God was moved, only that He was provoked to allow a ruin that would be, in the end, 'without cause.' The moral weight is placed on the accuser's pressing, not on Job's conduct.

The verb barak, which usually means to bless, is used here as a delicate way to say curse. Satan predicts that Job will 'curse You to Your face,' Job 2:5, and Job's wife says 'Curse God and die,' Job 2:9, where the BSB footnote gives 'Or Bless.' The same euphemism appears when false witnesses accuse Naboth of having 'cursed both God and the king,' 1 Kings 21:10 and 21:13. The word choice reflects a reluctance to say the thing outright. Bless and curse lie a short distance apart, which is exactly what the wager is about.

The verb in 'He still retains his integrity,' Job 2:3, is machazik, 'holds fast.' Job's wife uses the same participle in Job 2:9, 'Do you still retain your integrity?' What God offers as praise she recasts as stubbornness. Job will take the word back in Job 27:5-6, where he vows to 'cling to my righteousness and never let go.'

Job's answer turns on tov and ra, 'good' and 'adversity,' Job 2:10. The second is the ordinary word for bad, whether calamity or evil, and its use with God as the giver is what makes the sentence daring. It does not mean that God is the author of sin, but that no misfortune falls outside His hand.

Finally, the friends came to nud and to nacham, translated 'sympathize' and 'comfort,' Job 2:11. The first verb belongs to a root that can mean to shake the head or to wander, the body language of pity. The pair appears again in Job 42:11, where the family 'consoled him and comforted him,' and the echo frames the whole book in comfort, and turns Job's later complaint that his friends are 'miserable comforters' into a judgment on what came between.

One textual note. The Septuagint, the Greek translation, expands Job 2:9 into a long speech by Job's wife, full of her own grief. That expansion is not in the Hebrew, but it shows that early readers saw her not as a villain but as a broken woman.

typology.type: The righteous sufferer afflicted 'without cause,' Job 2:3
typology.fulfillment: Job is struck by an enemy while God Himself calls him blameless, and the affliction has no root in his own guilt. In Christ the pattern becomes exact. Jesus applies to Himself the words 'They hated Me without reason,' John 15:25, quoting a psalm of the righteous sufferer, Psalm 69:4, and Pilate, Judas and the centurion all call Him innocent, Matthew 27:4 and Luke 23:47. Job's innocence is real but relative, and God will still address him. Jesus is the only one whose innocence is absolute, so His suffering is not only undeserved but substitutionary, 1 Peter 3:18.

typology.type: Satan's sifting by permission, and the boundary of life, Job 2:6
typology.fulfillment: Satan can do nothing to Job until God grants the ground, and then only to the line God draws. Jesus tells Peter that Satan 'has asked to sift each of you like wheat' and adds that He has prayed for Peter, Luke 22:31-32. The escalation is that Job's protection is only a spoken boundary, while the disciples have a Mediator praying by name. In Christ the accuser's final case is silenced, for he 'has been thrown down,' Revelation 12:10. The type falls short because Job never learns of the boundary or of an advocate, and in this chapter no one prays for him.

typology.type: The counsellor who would divert the suffering servant, Job 2:9
typology.fulfillment: Job's wife offers a way out that would end the ordeal by ending the faith. Peter offers something similar when he says 'Far be it from You, Lord! This shall never happen to You!' and is answered, 'Get behind Me, Satan,' Matthew 16:22-23. In Gethsemane Jesus refuses a way out in the same spirit as Job: 'Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?' John 18:11. Both echo the question 'Should we accept from God only good and not adversity?' The correspondence deepens because in Jesus the cup is chosen for the sake of others, not endured in ignorance.

typology.type: Presence without words in the ash heap, Job 2:13
typology.fulfillment: The friends give what Scripture calls sympathy, coming and sitting with a man in ruin. It is real but partial, because they cannot enter his condition. The letter to the Hebrews says that in Christ 'we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses,' Hebrews 4:15, one who 'offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears,' Hebrews 5:7. The friends sit beside the ash heap; the Son of God enters it. The type also breaks down where Christ's sympathy never gives way to accusation, as the friends' will.

study.christ:
Job 2 leads to Christ first by contrast between two men on the same ground. Job is called 'blameless and upright' by God Himself, Job 2:3, and yet he is handed to the Accuser. The book will show that he is not sinless, for God will speak to him and he will repent in dust and ashes. The one of whom the same words are true without qualification is Jesus, who 'had done no violence, nor was any deceit in His mouth,' Isaiah 53:9. Where Job's innocence lets the reader see what suffering without cause looks like, Christ's innocence makes suffering redemptive. The same Isaiah passage says 'it was the LORD's will to crush Him,' Isaiah 53:10, and that He was 'stricken by God, struck down and afflicted,' Isaiah 53:4. The friends' error in the coming chapters, to read affliction as proof of guilt, is exactly the error the crowd made at the cross.

It leads to Christ by the body. Satan's second test moves from what Job owns to the flesh and bones themselves, Job 2:5. In the Gospels the enemy's assault on Jesus comes at the point of bodily weakness as well, after forty days without food, Luke 4:2, and its climax is the flesh nailed to a cross. The letter to the Hebrews says He took on our flesh and blood so that through death He might destroy the one who holds the power of death, Hebrews 2:14. Job's body is spared unto death; Christ's is not, and in the giving of it the accuser is answered for good.

It leads to Christ by refusal of the shortcut. Job's wife sees the cost of faithfulness and proposes an exit. Jesus meets the same shape of temptation when Peter tries to turn Him from the cross, Matthew 16:22-23, and in the garden He accepts the cup, John 18:11. Satan's claim that no one serves God for nothing is met by the Son who serves God at the greatest cost and receives nothing in return but the Father's approval.

It also leads to Christ by the comfort that finally works. The friends arrive, weep, tear their robes and sit, but they cannot bear what Job bears. Christ is called 'a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief,' Isaiah 53:3, and Hebrews says He is a high priest who was 'tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin,' Hebrews 4:15. The wounded Job needed someone to enter his suffering, and the New Testament shows that the Son of God did.

A warning keeps the reading honest. Job is not a disguised Christ, and his boils are not a coded prophecy. He is a real man who suffers, complains and is later rebuked. The links above rest on the New Testament's own use of the themes, chiefly the innocent sufferer, the accuser defeated, and the Mediator who prays. What Job 2 supplies is the problem, an innocent person under the accuser's hand with no visible reason and no advocate in sight, and the pattern to which the gospel gives its answer.
study.god:
The chapter first shows a God whose confidence in His servant is open and unashamed. He is the one who brings up Job in the council, twice, and gives the verdict before the test: 'no one on earth like him,' Job 2:3. It would be easy to read the council as a cold arrangement, but God speaks of Job as 'My servant,' a title of honour, and He puts His own reputation on the line for Job's sake. The doctrine of divine pride in a creature begins here.

It shows a God who is sovereign over the enemy without being the enemy's partner. Satan cannot act until God permits, and cannot pass a line God sets, Job 2:6. Yet Satan is not a puppet. The text says he 'went out from the presence of the LORD and infected Job,' Job 2:7, and the phrase leaves the assault as his act. Scripture holds two things together without merging them: nothing happens outside God's hand, and the evil done remains the accuser's own.

It shows a God who takes a real risk with His servant and yet remains just. God admits that Satan incited Him 'without cause,' Job 2:3, a phrase that keeps the innocence of Job in view at the very moment the affliction is granted. The text refuses the easy answer that suffering is always deserved and also refuses to say more than it says. God does not explain to Job in this chapter what is happening, and He does not protect him from it. The tension between His goodness and Job's pain is left standing.

It shows a God who is not diminished by human doubt. The wager is not a test of whether God is good enough to be served; it is a test of whether service to Him can survive the removal of every reward. Job's answer, 'Should we accept from God only good and not adversity?' Job 2:10, affirms that both good and adversity come from one hand, a line that agrees with Isaiah 45:7 and Deuteronomy 32:39, where God says 'I wound and I heal.' That hand is never described as capricious, only as beyond Job's view.

And it shows a God who wants to be served for Himself. The question 'Does Job fear God for nothing?' Job 1:9 asks whether God is worth loving apart from His gifts. The answer of the whole Bible is yes, since He is the gift.

For worship, the chapter teaches us to let God be God when our own hands are empty. Praise is not an investment. The one who receives good from God's hand and adversity from the same hand learns to say, with the psalmist, that God Himself is the portion, Psalm 73:26. The chapter also teaches us to trust that the God who sets a limit on the accuser has not left us to him, even when we cannot see the line.

crossReferences.note: The first council, which chapter 2 mirrors line for line. Comparing them shows the escalation: in Job 1:12 the limit was 'do not lay a hand on him,' and in Job 2:6 it becomes 'spare his life.' God's commendation, Satan's answer and the permission are in the same order, but the target has moved from what Job has to what Job is.

Job's first response, 'The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away. Blessed be the name of the LORD.' The narrator adds that he did not sin or charge God with wrongdoing. Job 2:10 is the second answer to the same test, and it sharpens the first by adding adversity to the list of things received from God.

The covenant curse of 'painful, incurable boils' from the soles of the feet to the top of the head uses the same Hebrew word for boils and nearly the same wording as Job 2:7. The echo makes Job look like a man under Moses' curses, which is why his friends will assume he is.

Satan stands at the right hand of Joshua the high priest to accuse him, and the LORD rebukes him. It confirms the role of the Accuser in a courtroom scene, and shows the same God who allows the accuser in Job as the one who silences him for the sake of His chosen.

Jesus tells Peter that Satan asked to sift him like wheat and that He has prayed for Peter's faith. The permission-and-limit structure of Job returns, now with the difference that a named Advocate stands in prayer beside the one being tested.

Paul's thorn in the flesh is a 'messenger of Satan' given to keep him from pride, yet the Lord answers his pleas with grace rather than removal. It shows a New Testament sufferer living inside the same reality as Job: affliction that is Satan's tool and God's instrument at once.

James points to Job's perseverance and 'the outcome from the Lord,' concluding that 'the Lord is full of compassion and mercy.' He reads Job 2's endurance in light of Job 42, and reminds readers that the purpose of the affliction, hidden in the chapter, was in the end kind.

The servant is 'a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief' and is 'stricken by God, struck down and afflicted.' The likeness to Job on the ash heap is strong, and the difference is what the passage adds: 'Surely He took on our infirmities and carried our sorrows.'

Joseph mourned his father for seven days, the ordinary span of grief. The friends' seven days of silence in Job 2:13 follow the same custom, so their silence reads as respect owed to the dead and dying, not embarrassment.

After the whole story the relatives 'consoled him and comforted him over all the adversity.' The same pair of verbs that described the friends' purpose in Job 2:11 returns, so the book of Job begins and ends in comfort, and the middle asks what real comfort requires.

study.oneStory:
Genesis 3 supplied the enemy and Job 2 shows him at work in a later age. The serpent who questioned God's word in the garden, 'Did God really say?' Genesis 3:1, is here the Accuser who questions God's servant: 'Does Job fear God for nothing?' Job 1:9. Both attack by doubting motive, and both operate under God's permission. Job 2 answers what Genesis 3 leaves open: whether a person could hold to God when the tree is not in view and there is nothing to gain.

The chapter also looks backward to Adam in another way. In Eden the first man was surrounded by every good and lost his place by listening to a lie. Job is stripped of every good and holds his place by refusing one. If the first Adam fell in the garden of plenty, this man is tested on a heap of ashes.

Forward, it sets up the great question the rest of Scripture will answer. Is there a righteous one who suffers and does not curse? Israel's psalms sing of such a person and Isaiah names him, the servant who 'had done no violence' and yet was crushed, Isaiah 53:9-10. Job's chapter is where the problem is stated at its sharpest, an innocent person under the accuser's hand with no visible reason. The gospel is the resolution, for Jesus meets the accuser and refuses the shortcut, and in dying breaks the accuser's power, Hebrews 2:14.

The friends' visit prepares another line of the story. Human comfort begins well and then fails, and the Bible will keep returning to the need for a comforter who can stay: the Lord who is near to the brokenhearted, Psalm 34:18, the Advocate whom Jesus promises, John 14:16, and the God who at last will wipe away every tear.

Finally the chapter ends where the whole story ends, with a promise that the accuser does not win. The heavenly voice in Revelation 12:10 declares that 'the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down.' In the new creation there will be no more affliction, no ash heap and no more death, Revelation 21:4, and the God who once allowed His servant to be tried will wipe away every tear.

sermon.title: Holding on to Your Faith in the Midst of Suffering: Job, Part 2
sermon.why: Piper walks directly through Job 2:6-10, showing that though Satan struck Job with sores, the text's own commentary traces the ultimate cause to God's sovereign hand, and that Job's reply, shall we receive good from God and not adversity, is the theological anchor for the whole chapter.

quiz.q: What decisive word does God use to describe Job's suffering when speaking to Satan?

options.text: Chinnam, without cause, ruling out the idea that Job's suffering was deserved.
options.note: God's own description in verse 3 closes off any theory of merited punishment before the friends ever speak.

options.text: That Satan incited Him to harm Job, though God still calls it undeserved.
options.note: True to the verse's wording, but less precise than naming the key word chinnam itself as the decisive term.

options.text: That the suffering was Satan's idea entirely, with no divine involvement.
options.note: Satan incites the test, but God permits and bounds it; God's sovereignty over the event is affirmed even as He names it undeserved.

options.text: That Job deserved some measure of correction.
options.note: God explicitly says the opposite, that Job was ruined without cause.

quiz.q: What is the meaning of Satan's proverb, 'skin for skin'?

options.text: That people will give up anything, even someone else's skin, to preserve their own life, implying Job has not yet truly been tested.
options.note: Satan argues that until Job's own body suffers, his devotion remains unproven.

options.text: That self-preservation is the deepest human motive, so only an attack on Job's own body will reveal the truth.
options.note: Captures Satan's underlying logic, though less precise than the exact wording of the proverb about trading skin for skin.

options.text: That Job would gladly trade his life for his children's lives.
options.note: This captures a partial idea of exchange, but misses Satan's specific point about self-preservation as the deepest human motive.

options.text: That Job's skin disease is a punishment for boasting.
options.note: The proverb is about self-preservation, not a specific judgment for boasting.

quiz.q: How does Job answer his wife's counsel to curse God and die?

options.text: By asking whether we should accept only good from God and not adversity, and the narrator affirms he did not sin in what he said.
options.note: Verse 10 gives Job's reply and the narrator's own verdict on it.

options.text: By rebuking her counsel as foolish and insisting we must accept adversity from God as well as good.
options.note: Correct in substance, though less precise than the narrator's own explicit verdict that Job did not sin in what he said.

options.text: By remaining completely silent and not responding at all.
options.note: Job gives a clear verbal answer, recorded in verse 10, rather than silence.

options.text: By cursing God as she suggested, but only privately.
options.note: The text explicitly says Job did not sin in what he said.

quiz.q: What do Job's three friends do first, before any speeches begin?

options.text: They weep aloud, tear their robes, throw dust on their heads, and then sit with him in silence for seven days and nights.
options.note: Verses 12 to 13 describe this as an act of real, costly sympathy before any words of counsel are offered.

options.text: They approach him, grieve visibly, and stay with him for an extended time before saying anything.
options.note: True in substance, though less specific than the exact seven days and nights of silence the text describes.

options.text: They immediately begin explaining why Job must have sinned.
options.note: That accusing counsel comes only later, starting in chapter 4; here they simply grieve and sit in silence.

options.text: They refuse to approach him because of his condition.
options.note: They come close enough to weep and sit with him, despite barely recognizing him.

quiz.q: Why is it significant that God twice affirms Job still holds his tummah, his integrity?

options.text: It shows Job's uprightness has survived both the loss of wealth and family and the loss of health, proving it was never dependent on comfort.
options.note: God's repeated affirmation in 2:3 tracks the escalation of the test and confirms Job's devotion is not transactional, directly answering Satan's original accusation in chapter 1.

options.text: It shows that God's earlier assessment of Job still stands even after far greater loss.
options.note: True as far as it goes, but less specific than naming exactly what has escalated, the loss of health after the loss of wealth and family.

options.text: It shows that Job never experienced any real doubt or struggle.
options.note: The coming chapters will show Job in deep anguish and doubt; integrity does not mean the absence of struggle.

options.text: It proves Job earned back God's favor through good behavior.
options.note: God's commendation precedes and does not depend on any new deeds; it is the same verdict repeated, not favor Job earns anew.

questions: Job says we must accept adversity from God's hand as readily as good. Where in your own life do you find that harder to actually live out than to say?

Job's friends' first and best gift was simply sitting with him in silence for seven days. Who in your life is suffering right now, and what would it cost you to sit with them before you try to explain anything?
Job's wife had lost the same children and the same fortune, yet the text leaves her grief largely unaddressed. How do you make room for the grief of others even when their words in pain trouble you?

God calls Job's suffering 'without cause,' closing the door on simple explanations. Where are you tempted to manufacture a reason for suffering, yours or someone else's, rather than sit with the fact that some suffering has no tidy explanation?
Job's integrity held through the loss of health as well as wealth. What would have to be stripped from your life before you discovered what your own faith is really resting on?

translationNotes.note: Without cause renders chinnam, a strong term meaning gratuitously or for no reason, used elsewhere for gifts given freely; here it underscores that Job's suffering was in no way earned.
Curse God and die uses the same euphemistic use of barak, bless, for curse found in chapter 1, softening the plain sense of the words at the point of greatest danger to God's honor in the text.

The BSB names all three friends together in one sentence; the underlying Hebrew lists their names and hometowns as a formal, almost legal introduction, marking their arrival as a significant event in the narrative.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched via the makor-scripture toolkit for Job 2:1-13. no other substantive changes were made to the verse text.
